title: Mobile and Embedded Computing
learningGoals: Define mobile and embedded computing and edge computing (on-device AI), and say why they matter.
Explain the constraints: battery and power, form factor, chipset and thermal limits, memory, compute (ARM), and communication and bandwidth, plus their impact.
Describe the smartphone as a computer: the SoC (CPU, GPU, NPU/TPU, DSP, ISP, modem, power management), ARM big.LITTLE, Google Tensor, the mobile GPU, and sensors.
Explain the Android architecture (apps → framework → runtime → HAL → Linux kernel), app sandboxing, the memory layout and app killing.

Explain the mobile as a client in a distributed system: APIs (REST, gRPC), HTTP(S) and JSON, stateless calls, latency and reliability fixes (retry, cache, batch), background threads and asynchronous programming.
sirStressed: "Understanding mobile devices = understanding the world's primary computing platform."
Edge computing / on-device AI (background blur, face detection) brings privacy and low latency. Big training stays in the cloud.

The constraints and their impact: battery (the screen and radios use the most), form factor, thermal throttling or shutdown, RAM 4–12 GB with limited swap, ARM with few cores, and a variable network. "Mind the constraints and optimise accordingly."
SoC: CPU, GPU, NPU/TPU, DSP, ISP, modem, power management. ARM big.LITTLE = performance + efficiency cores. Google Tensor (TPU, Titan).
Android stack: apps → framework → runtime → HAL → Linux kernel optimised for mobile. Sandboxing. The OS kills apps when RAM is full.

The mobile as a client: REST or gRPC APIs, HTTP methods, JSON, encryption against man-in-the-middle attacks, stateless calls. Retry + caching + batching. Background threads + asynchronous code keep the UI smooth.
commonTraps: Embedded = a computer inside a non-computer device (a washing machine), not just "small".
Edge computing = local processing, not "the edge of the cloud data centre".
big.LITTLE = a mix of high-performance and efficiency cores.
ISP = camera/image; DSP = audio/video signals; NPU/TPU = AI. Don't swap them.
In Android, the HAL sits between the runtime/framework and the Linux kernel. The kernel is at the bottom.
Thermal throttling lowers the CPU speed. It isn't a battery feature.
Stateless = the server doesn't remember earlier requests.
Network calls on the UI thread cause freezing. Use background threads and asynchronous code.
summary: Mobile (phones, tablets, watches; the most-used platform) and embedded (computing inside appliances, medical devices, IoT, Samsung Bespoke AI). Edge / on-device AI: privacy, low latency, offline (blur, face detection). Training stays in the cloud.

Constraints: battery (the screen and radios use the most; control background apps), form factor (no fan, fixed RAM), thermal (throttling, app kill, shutdown), memory (4–12 GB, limited swap, memory budget, OS kills apps), compute (ARM, few big cores, small caches), network (variable 2G–5G and Wi-Fi, switching). Optimise for the constraints.

Phone = a computer. SoC: CPU (ARM), GPU (shader cores; the CPU sends commands), NPU/TPU, DSP (audio/video), ISP (camera), modem, PMU. Snapdragon, Apple A-series, Exynos, Google Tensor (TPU, Mali GPU, Titan security).
ARM big.LITTLE: big performance + LITTLE efficiency cores, lower clock speeds, for balance.

Android: apps (Java/Kotlin) → framework → ART (bytecode) → HAL → Linux kernel (mobile-optimised). Sandboxed processes, limited background resources, the OS kills apps when RAM is full. Input: touch, voice, sensors (GPS, gyroscope, accelerometer, proximity, NFC), camera, microphone, Bluetooth.

Mobile as a client: login → auth server → API gateway → back end. REST or gRPC, HTTP GET/POST/DELETE, JSON, HTTPS encryption (defeats MITM), stateless calls. The cloud provides scaling and elasticity (Uber surge after flights land).

Problems: delay, weak signal, overload, packet loss, battery and data drain. Fixes: retry, caching, batching, fewer background processes. Responsiveness: background threads, a light UI thread, asynchronous programming (Kotlin coroutines).

List five constraints of mobile devices and one design response to each.
correctAnswers: Any five: Battery: limit background apps, optimise CPU/GPU use, dim or adapt the screen. Form factor: use a small, efficient SoC. Thermal: throttling, with the OS killing apps when needed. Memory (4–12 GB, limited swap): strict memory budgets, and the OS kills background apps. Compute (ARM, few cores): big.LITTLE, NPUs for AI, offloading to the cloud. Network variability: caching, retries, batching, and edge processing.

questions.prompt: What is app sandboxing in Android, and why is it needed?
correctAnswers: Sandboxing: each app runs in its own process with its own memory, isolated from the others. It can't access another app's memory or data without explicit permission granted through the OS. It's needed for security and privacy (a malicious app can't read your banking app's data) and stability (one crashing app doesn't bring down the others).

questions.prompt: A food-delivery app freezes whenever the user taps "Track order" on a weak 3G signal in a train, and it drains the battery. Suggest four improvements.
correctAnswers: Any four: Make the network call on a background thread with asynchronous code (coroutines), so the UI thread stays responsive. Cache the last known order status and location, and show it immediately. Retry with back-off on failure. Batch or reduce polling (fewer, larger requests, or push notifications), which saves the battery and data. Compress the JSON payloads. Reduce background processes.

questions.prompt: Give three reasons why a phone acts as a client and leaves heavy work to cloud servers, and two reasons why some AI is now done on the device instead.
correctAnswers: Client reasons: Limited compute, RAM and battery. Data lives centrally (orders, maps, accounts) and needs real-time updates. The cloud gives scalability and elasticity and runs heavy ML inference and storage. On-device reasons: - Privacy (data stays on the phone). - Low latency and offline use (no network round trip), using NPUs or TPUs such as Google Tensor.
